Credit Cards Balance Transfer Credit Cards

Best Balance Transfer Credit Cards in [September 2026]

Balance transfer credit cards offer introductory 0% APR periods that often give you between 12 and 21 months to pay off your debt without accruing interest. Here are the top cards we recommend for balance transfer intro APRs.

By Lauren Graves and Ashley Donohoe, MBA, CFLP®, CFEI®, FPWMP® , Edited by Tracy Odell
Updated Sept. 22, 2026
Fact checked

A balance transfer involves transferring a credit card balance from one credit card to another in order to pay off the original card. If the new credit card has a lower APR, a balance transfer may help you get out of high-interest debt faster. In some cases, you can start with no APR at all on the new card, which is known as a 0% intro APR offer.

The best balance transfer credit cards give you a 0% intro APR for 12 months or more, even as long as 18 or 21 months, which may give you enough time to pay off your balance without accruing more interest charges. Citi and Wells Fargo stand out among credit issuers for offering many top balance transfer cards, but you can also find excellent options from Discover and other issuers, depending on what you're looking for.

Here are the balance transfer cards we recommend, who each one is best for, and how to choose the right card for you.

Our take: Citi dominates the balance transfer card market thanks primarily to the Citi Simplicity and this card, the Citi Diamond Preferred. Like the Simplicity, the Diamond Preferred gives the gift of time, but a fair bit more of it. Offering a 0% intro APR on balance transfers for 21 months from date of account opening (then 16.74% - 27.49% (Variable)), it ties with only a few others for one of the longest balance transfer offers. But it isn't the best all-around intro APR card because its intro APR on new purchases is much shorter.

The Citi Diamond Preferred stands out from the others on our list for its lowest possible regular APR. If you're realistic about your debt payoff timeline and realize that you might actually need longer than 21 months to get your balance to zero, you'll be glad for a potentially lower regular rate when that kicks in after the intro APR period is up. Only the most creditworthy applicants typically qualify for the Diamond Preferred Card's lowest APR, but even a slightly lower minimum and maximum matter when you're talking about potentially adding to your debt.

Drawbacks: This card is a great balance transfer credit card, but it has less that sets it apart than the Citi Simplicity. It charges late fees and doesn't offer quite as long of an intro APR on purchases.

Our take: The Citi Double Cash is the first card on our list to earn rewards, and it made quite the splash when it launched in 2014 by letting you earn up to 2% cash back on everything (1% cash back when you buy, plus an additional 1% as you pay for those purchases).

The Double Cash has one of the most unusual reward-earning structures out there, because you don't earn all of your rewards right away. Instead, you earn half when you spend, and half when you pay off that spending. This could be exactly the motivation you need to keep your credit card bill paid, especially if you've only recently joined the good-credit club (note that this card recommends good or excellent credit). Plus, the points you earn are more flexible than your average cash back because they're Citi ThankYou® Points. You can redeem them for everything from statement credits and direct deposits to travel and online shopping.

Drawbacks: This card's balance transfer promotion is a little short compared to true balance transfer cards, though still longer than most rewards credit cards. It also doesn't have an intro APR offer for new purchases at all, so even though it's great for regular spending, it's not a good choice for avoiding interest on regular spending. And if you can't keep your credit card bill paid off, you won't earn the full up to 2% and could hurt your credit, which is uniquely punishing.

Rounding out the card's potential to save you money is its Balance transfer fee applies and policy to forgive your first late payment (after that, up to $41). We'd still strongly caution against missing payments and recommend scheduling automatic payments if you're able, but even a tiny bit of wiggle room on this can help your budget (though it won't protect your credit, so be careful out there).

If you might exceed that quarterly cap, choose a different card.

How to successfully do a balance transfer

Using a balance transfer card is just one strategy to potentially pay off debt, but opening one isn't a silver bullet. To take full advantage of intro APR offers on balance transfer cards and make as much progress on your credit card debt as possible, follow these steps to transfer a balance from one card to another.

  • Request a balance transfer
    • Remember to factor in fees
  • Repay your balance
  • Avoid excessive spending

Request a balance transfer

Once you've been approved for a balance transfer card, you can initiate a balance transfer with your new issuer.

You can typically do this in one of three ways:

  • Online
  • Through the mobile app
  • Over the phone

You'll need to provide details about the debt you're transferring, including the amount and account information for the cards or loans it's coming from.

Don't forget balance transfer fees

Balance transfers aren't free — they have balance transfer fees. These fees typically range from 3% to 5% of the transferred balance. So transferring a $1,000 balance could cost you between $30 and $50, tacked on to your new balance.

Calculate whether a balance transfer is worth it. To do this, look at the interest you're currently being charged and compare it to the balance transfer fee. If you would end up saving more on interest than you'd pay for the fee, a balance transfer could be worth it.

Editor's note
In some cases, you can also request a balance transfer check. This is a physical check from your new credit card issuer that you can use to borrow against your credit limit and repay your original creditor, if you choose. We don't recommend using these checks in most instances because they can come with different fees, benefits, and interest rates than balance transfer credit cards, and they come with the added inconvenience of having to send payments yourself.

Repay your balance

After the transfer, focus on paying off your transferred balance.

If your card has a 0% intro APR period, try to repay the entire balance (or as much as you can manage) before the period ends.

Example

If you open a new card with a 0% intro APR on balance transfers for 18 months, see if you can fit regular payments for the total balance into your budget for 18 months. Maybe you're transferring $5,000 and can afford a $300 monthly payment, which would let you repay your balance in a little over 16 months.

Try to pay more than the required minimum payment each statement period, and consider scheduling automatic payments for as long as the introductory APR applies.

The example below shows why paying more than the minimum matters, and how avoiding interest during a 0% intro APR period can help you get out of debt much faster.

By putting as much as possible toward your balance during the promotional period, you can make meaningful progress before interest starts accruing again.

Avoid excessive spending

While a credit card balance transfer could help you pay off debt, it's important to use it responsibly. Balance transfers work best when you avoid running up new debt and try to pay off the balance before the introductory rate expires.

It's also important to note that, although many balance transfer credit cards also offer 0% intro APRs on new purchases, some don't. So you can start accruing interest right away on purchases, even if your transferred balance won't.

Perspectives
Allison Weston
Writer and Editor
Allie began her career doing marketing research for financial institutions, then transitioned to working for a large financial advisory firm. She found her passion in the world of publishing, where she helps readers make smart financial decisions.

How I used a balance transfer card to manage a large expense

I had an upcoming surgery that cost $8,000 out of pocket. After researching, I decided that using a balance transfer credit card would be the best option to pay for the surgery over time. I applied and qualified for a balance transfer credit card that also offers long introductory APR on new purchases, and I was able to easily break the total into monthly payments over a year.

I also took advantage of my remaining available credit and transferred existing debt from another high-interest credit card. Ultimately, both of these benefits saved me hundreds of dollars in interest charges and allowed me to pay down debt faster.

Remember, while a credit card balance transfer can be a great tool to manage and pay off debt, it's important to use it responsibly. Balance transfers work best when you avoid running up new debt on the card and try to pay off the balance before the introductory rate expires.

How much could you save with a balance transfer credit card?

A balance transfer credit card can make a big difference if you're carrying high-interest credit card debt. The example below shows how transferring a $5,000 balance from a card with a 22% APR to a card offering 0% intro APR for 18 months could reduce your total cost and help you pay off the debt sooner — even after accounting for a typical balance transfer fee.

By moving a balance to a card with a 0% introductory APR, you can temporarily avoid interest charges and put more of your payment toward the principal.

How to pick the right balance transfer card for you

Many credit cards are balance transfer cards, but they vary widely. Follow these steps to compare balance transfer offers:

  1. Consider your credit: Your credit helps determine whether you're approved for a card. Many top balance transfer cards require good or excellent credit.
  2. Focus on intro APR offer lengths: Depending on your debt, you may want a card with a longer balance transfer period. Many start at 12 months.
  3. Check regular APRs: When intro APRs end, regular APRs kick in. To be safe, look for cards with low interest rates to potentially avoid extra debt.
  4. Don't forget balance transfer fees: Most credit cards charge balance transfer fees between 3% and 5% of the amount you transfer.
  5. Research issuers: You usually can't transfer debt between cards from the same issuer. For example, if you have the Chase Freedom Unlimited®, you can't transfer your balance to another Chase credit card.
  6. Compare rewards programs: Some balance transfer cards earn rewards, some don't. Often, if you want the best balance transfer offer possible, you won't earn rewards, and cards without rewards offer little ongoing value.

Pros and cons of balance transfer credit cards

Pros Cons
Could help you repay debt faster by lowering interest burden Often charge fees between 3% and 5%
Intro APR periods often start at 12 months High regular APRs apply after intro APRs end
Many don't have annual fees Often require at least good credit
Consolidating debt can simplify repayment May not earn rewards or offer many benefits
Could help your credit in the long-term May not qualify for the credit limit you need

Alternatives to balance transfer credit cards

If you look at those cons and drawbacks and decide that a balance transfer card isn't the right choice for you right now, you have other options. Here are some alternatives to consider in different circumstances. Just note that, as you're comparing these, they won't be right for everyone, either.

Personal loans

A personal loan might be right for you if:

  • You need more time to pay down your balance than balance transfer cards offer
  • You wouldn't be approved for a balance transfer card
  • You wouldn't qualify for a high enough credit limit

Debt consolidation personal loans are a common debt repayment strategy, and rightfully so. The concept is similar to balance transfer cards: You join all or some of your debt under one new roof for easier repayment (and interest savings, if you're doing it right), and you pay off your original debts with the loan proceeds. You turn disjointed debts into one big, happy family that you make one monthly payment toward. Many personal loans are available in terms of one to seven years for up to $50,000 or more.

One significant benefit of personal loans over balance transfer credit cards is fixed interest, which means fixed repayments. While credit cards have variable APRs that can change at any time, without warning, personal loans lock in interest rates when you open them. These rates tend to be lower than credit card APRs, although your loan's APR depends on your creditworthiness and the loan you're taking out. But if you have good enough credit to qualify for a balance transfer credit card, you likely have good enough credit to qualify for a personal loan.

One major caveat: You repay personal loans in fixed monthly installments, meaning that you don't have the flexibility to skip repayments when funds are tight. You'll need to commit to those repayments for the full length of the term, or risk penalties, fees, and much darker stuff (such as defaulting on the loan).

Home equity loans or HELOCs

A home equity loan or HELOC might be right for you if:

  • You have significant home equity
  • You need more time than balance transfer cards offer

Using your house as collateral to borrow money, like balance transfers, comes with disadvantages. The first is in the first half of that sentence. Moving unsecured debt from credit cards to secured debt opens you up to the possibility of losing the asset used to secure the debt, which is, in this case, your home.

But if you're confident in your ability to keep making monthly payments and you want to spread out those payments over more time than a balance transfer credit card would give you to avoid interest, a home equity loan or home equity line of credit (HELOC) could be worth considering. They offer rates that can be much lower than credit card APRs, even personal loan APRs, for terms between five and 30 years.

Credit counseling or debt management plans

Credit counseling or a debt management plan might be right for you if:

  • You need more support in repaying your debt
  • You have a habit of overspending
  • You tried balance transfers and other debt repayment strategies before

If the reason you're nervous about balance transfers is that you aren't sure you'd be able to conquer your debt with one, your problem might not be with the balance transfer at all. It might be with your debt and your plan for repaying it. 

If you want more help with getting out of debt, maybe because you've tried different debt repayment strategies before to no avail or because your debt just feels insurmountable, it might be time to recruit some outside help. Credit counseling is one option. It involves speaking with a professional, often from a nonprofit, about your situation. They'll walk you through your options and often support you with everything from budgeting to your credit, plus help you break down your debt repayment. This service, which usually costs money, could be enough to get some people on the right track. 

But if your credit counselor feels it's the right move, they might suggest a debt management plan. This structures your debt repayment into a concrete, manageable plan and often involves negotiating with your creditors to try to lower your balances and/or rates.

FAQs

How long do balance transfers take?

The answer to this varies by card issuer, but in general, you can expect your credit card balance to transfer over to your new card within about a week. However, the process can take up to 21 days. 

Sometimes cards with balance transfer offers require you to transfer your balance within a certain number of days of account opening. Make sure you keep an eye out for details like that when you decide which balance transfer card to apply for. 

How much can you transfer on a balance transfer credit card?

How much you can transfer onto a new credit card depends on your credit limit. For example, if you have $10,000 in credit card debt and the new 0% intro APR credit card has a credit limit of $6,000, then you won't be able to transfer over the full balance.

You also need to account for the balance transfer fee. Your transfer amount plus the balance transfer fee must be less than the total credit line available on your new balance transfer card.

Can you make multiple balance transfers?

While you can complete multiple balance transfers — as long as you transfer to a card at a different lender — that can be a sign there are bigger issues with your debt. While a balance transfer can make you feel like you're managing your debt better, doing more than one balance transfer signals that you may have a spending or cash flow problem.

Before doing another balance transfer, take a hard look at your credit card statements and identify areas where you can cut back. It's also a good idea to create a budget for yourself and find ways to boost your income so you can regain control of your money. 

If you have multiple balances you want to transfer, you might also want to consider a personal loan to consolidate your debt. 

Are balance transfers worth it?

Balance transfers can be worth it if they save you money on interest. If you transfer a balance from a high-interest credit card to a card with a lower interest rate, then you could be better off in the long run. A lengthy period of time with less interest could help you pay down your credit card debt and manage your finances better. If you're considering a card with an intro balance transfer APR, take a good look at the card details before you apply.

And if you're interested in perks beyond a 0% intro APR offer on balance transfers, many cards also offer limited-time introductory offers on new purchases, as well as cashback rewards, bonus points on certain spending categories, flexible redemption options, or benefits like lucrative sign-up bonuses, no foreign transaction fees, or extended warranty coverage. These perks can be useful if you want to use your new card to make a large purchase and pay it off over time.

Bottom line

If you're struggling with high-interest debt, then an introductory balance transfer offer could help you save money on interest and pay off your balances faster. The best balance transfer cards give you at least the first year to pay down your debt interest-free, which makes them an effective personal finance tool for managing debt.

Methodology

How we chose the best balance transfer credit cards

To select the best balance transfer cards, we looked for cards that offer 0% intro APR offers on balance transfers across a range of issuers. From this list of options, we chose the featured cards based on the following:

  • Annual fees: We chose to only include cards with no annual fee on this list. We don't believe cards that carry an annual fee are a good fit for people who are looking to pay down a balance while avoiding interest but it’s not typical for balance transfer cards to carry annual fees anyway.
  • Balance transfer periods: 0% intro APR periods typically range from 12 to 21 months for balance transfers. We considered cards across this range but gave preference to those with the longest balance transfer intro periods, because giving yourself more time to avoid costly interest payments can increase the amount of debt you're able to pay off. Some cards on this list allow for up to 21 months of interest-free balance transfers, though a longer intro period is often a trade-off; the longer an intro offer, the fewer other benefits a card generally offers.
  • Other benefits: While an intro APR period is enough to justify getting a balance transfer card for many, the longer an intro offer, the fewer other benefits a card generally offers. In recognition of this, we gave preference to cards that offer benefits and perks extending beyond an intro APR period. We looked for cards that offer cash back rewards or a welcome offer, among other perks. The opportunity to earn ongoing rewards can increase a credit card's long-term value and make you more likely to keep using it after your intro APR period ends.

The cards on this list were also given individual star ratings using FinanceBuzz’s card ratings methodology. While more than a dozen cards from prominent issuers were considered, we did not evaluate all available credit cards in the market.
